content_html_sanitized:
Posted April 10, 2001
Not a movie review by Richard Cowan

After reading about it for months, I finally got around to seeing " Traffic " this weekend. It was every bit as good as I had heard, but I am still glad that I saw it after its impact on the public discourse.

When one sees a movie so late in its run, there is always the problem that one knows everything about it, so there is no suspense. In this case, I went to see it knowing all about the impact that it has had.

Most movies are about myth-making. However, " Traffic " is just the opposite. It is about myth-shattering. In that regard " Traffic " was enormously successful. But why did it have such an impact? It was a great flick, but…

Certainly there were no revelations in the film that would be news to anyone paying attention to the debate about the Drug War over the last few years. Any number of respected intellectuals have articulated the arguments " Traffic " presented in cinematic shorthand. The facts are there for anyone to see. Does it really take a movie with Senators in cameo roles to get Senators in real-life to acknowledge the obvious?

Without taking anything away from its cinematic quality, I think that the real key to its impact, as opposed to its boffo box office, was great timing. It opened just as criticism of the Drug War had become acceptable. Had it come out only a few years ago nothing would really have been any different in the plot, or the box office. However, only movie reviewers – not pundits -- would have written about it.

Slowly over the last few years DEAland has begun to experience the late Soviet phenomenon called glasnost -- the ability to publicly criticize the state ideology, prohibitionism. " Traffic " both benefited from and facilitated this process. Talking about a hit movie is acceptable. The Soviets had their poets. DEAland has Hollywood.

Like the original glasnost, this criticism is supposed to find a way to make the system work. The objective is not to end the system, but to find a better way, perestroika, literally restructuring. Of course, it did not work out in the USSR, because Communism was unworkable. And it will not work here, because prohibition is not just a failure, but a counterproductive fraud that cannot withstand honest criticism.

As everyone must know by now, there were three plot lines in " Traffic. " I was most moved by the parts shot in Mexico. I have a great love for that country, and I am particularly outraged by the devastation it – and Colombia, where I spent my 21st birthday – must suffer as a result of the Drug War. It is even more offensive that DEAland politicians try to blame those countries for the consequences of our policies. Blaming the victims on a geopolitical scale…

Most reviewers and pundits, however, seem to grasp the impossibility of stemming the supply, which was the focus of both the Mexican and California segments. Even before " Traffic " there was a growing recognition that this would never work, and there were already moves to end the offensive " certification " process, especially for Mexico.

On the other hand, many people seem to miss some points about the segment about the Drug Czar and his daughter. Michael Douglas’ character, like William Bennett, was a visible consumer of alcohol, although unlike Bennett, who was on nicotine maintenance when he was Czar, he does not look like a lush and is not obese. But the Czar’s mild alcohol dependence was a consistent subplot.

His very bright daughter and her friends were the profoundly alienated children of privilege. The hypocrisy of the system was not lost on them. They benefited from it, but resented it. This is not uncommon for children of privilege. The same process was at work during the Vietnam war in which the children of the poor did most – but not all -- of the dying, and the children of privilege did most --but not all -- of the protesting.

Although the story-line seemed have her descend with improbable speed into poly-drug abuse, her mother acknowledged that she had known for six months that she was " experimenting. " (That politically correct word was the target of some barbed comments.)

Mexican cops, honest and dishonest, mean little to DEAland politicians. California and Mexican " drug lords " mean even less. But the problems of their own children are something that they can relate to. It is a cliché that parents should talk to their children about " drugs " – but it would seem that " Traffic " gave politicians an occasion to talk to their children about drug prohibition, and a few seemed to have learned something.

On the other hand it is possible to give " Traffic " too much credit. As noted, it was the beneficiary of perfect timing. However, it really was not revolutionary. It did not point to the way out of the quagmire. In stead it took up the currently fashionable emphasis on treatment. Douglas’s Czar asks why no one representing " treatment " was on his visit to the Mexican border. Why should someone representing " treatment " visit the border? Are we going to " treat " the poor " mules " who get caught taking the greatest risk for the least money?

Although the movie ends with the Czar’s daughter in " treatment, " and happy endings are good box office, the fact remains that we cannot mass produce good treatment programs any more than we can mass produce " criminal justice. " A lot of treatment programs are vicious rackets that exploit the victims of prohibition.

So " Traffic " was a phenomenon because it told us what we were ready to hear. There is a larger story that DEAland is now ready to hear. The greatest weakness of the film was its failure to deal with the subject of marijuana prohibition. The screenplay deserved its Oscar, and only so much can be covered in one film, but marijuana prohibition is the heart of the Drug War.

Movies take several years and many millions to make, but perhaps one about marijuana prohibition is working its way through the process. If not, then I look forward to seeing one that will tell us what happened -- after the war on us is over.
